expected_evidence: Ice-core geochemical records from Greenland (GISP2, NGRIP, NEEM) tested for platinum-group-element (Pt, Ir) anomalies, magnetic spherules, and nanodiamonds at the ~12.9 ka BP horizon, with multiple independent labs failing to reproduce the originally reported anomalies

Peer-reviewed replication/rebuttal literature (e.g. Pigati et al. 2012, Daulton et al. 2010, van Hoesel et al. 2012/2014, Boslough et al. 2012 critiques) documenting failed attempts to confirm the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis markers
Sediment core and terrestrial site re-analyses across North America/Europe showing inconsistent or absent nanodiamond/spherule signals used to argue against a coherent impact layer
Absence of a confirmed impact crater or unambiguous shocked-quartz/tektite field correlated to ~10,950 BC, cited as corroborating negative evidence
Meta-analyses or review articles summarizing the scientific consensus shift away from the cosmic-impact interpretation of YD onset cooling
response.rationale: The hypothesis describes a scientific refutation event (failed independent replication of the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis), which is conceptually a modern (20th-21st century CE) scientific process, not an event that occurred 'in' -10950 BP itself. The interval given (-10950) actually marks the dated YD onset layer being studied, not the date of the refutation debate — this is a temporal category mismatch worth flagging. Using the supplied period/evidence detectability table under 'younger-dryas', the most relevant channels are geological (0.65) and material (0.35) evidence from Greenland ice cores and associated sediment archives, since these are the physical substrates where impact-proxy replication attempts would leave traces; textual detectability for the ancient period itself is 0.0, which correctly reflects that no contemporaneous ~10,950 BC written record could exist, but this is largely irrelevant because the refutation debate's real evidentiary record (journal articles, replication data) is a modern textual/scientific artifact outside this ancient-period table entirely. Based on model-prior (unverified, from training recall rather than the evidence text provided): there was indeed a real, well-documented multi-year scientific controversy over the Younger Dryas Impact Hypothesis in which several independent groups reported failing to replicate platinum, nanodiamond, and spherule anomalies at YD-onset horizons, including in Greenland-adjacent and North American sites — so the underlying claim is plausible and evidence of this type does exist in the actual literature, even though it doesn't fit neatly into the ancient-period detectability schema given. Averaging the relevant physical-proxy channels (geological/material) rather than the inapplicable ancient textual/oral channels, I suggest a moderate-to-good detectability adjustment (~0.55), reflecting that ice-core and sediment-based replication evidence is reasonably preservable and searchable, while acknowledging that the low textual detectability score in this table is a mismatch artifact of forcing a modern scientific dispute into an ancient-period evidence framework rather than a true indicator of absent evidence.
